---
title: "Performance"
---

This page shows how well EvoDAG classifies 30 problems and how it compares with the classifiers of [scikit-learn](http://scikit-learn.org) and with the selection schemes described in [Selection](selection.qmd). The numbers were measured once and are copied here; they are not computed when the site is built.

## The setup

* **Problems.** 30 classification problems of the [UCI repository](https://archive.ics.uci.edu), listed below with the size of the training and of the test part, the number of variables and the number of classes. The problems that come with a training and a test set use them; the others are split in 70 % of the examples of each class for training and 30 % for test.
* **Measure.** Macro-F1 on the test part (the mean over the classes of the F1 of each class; 1 is perfect). Systems are compared by the *average rank* over the problems: on each problem the systems are ranked by macro-F1, 1 is the best, and the ranks are averaged. Lower is better. The Friedman test says whether the systems of a table can be told apart at all.
* **EvoDAG.** An ensemble of 30 models (`EvoDAGE`) with the default parameters of classification, in which only the selection parameters change from one EvoDAG system to another; the class is the majority vote of the 30 models and there is no time limit. Nothing is tuned.
* **scikit-learn.** The 16 classifiers `AdaBoost`, `BernoulliNB`, `DecisionTree`, `ExtraTrees`, `GaussianNB`, `GradientBoosting`, `KNeighbors`, `LinearSVC`, `LogisticRegression`, `MLP`, `NearestCentroid`, `PassiveAggressive`, `Perceptron`, `RandomForest`, `SGD` and `SVC`, each with the default parameters of its class.

The results differ from those printed in the selection article for the same configurations; the reason is explained in [the note on the first argument](selection.qmd#the-first-argument-is-the-reference).

## EvoDAG against the classifiers of scikit-learn

The table has the 21 systems: the default EvoDAG, `agr-rnd`, four other EvoDAG configurations that [the next section](#the-selection-schemes) explains, and the 16 classifiers of scikit-learn. Friedman test over the 30 problems: p = 4.53e-48.

|System|Family|Average rank|
|:---|:---|---:|
|`ExtraTrees`|scikit-learn|4.9|
|`GradientBoosting`|scikit-learn|5.5|
|`RandomForest`|scikit-learn|5.5|
|`agr-rnd`|EvoDAG|6.0|
|`rnd-rnd`|EvoDAG|6.2|
|`fit-fit`|EvoDAG|6.9|
|`nvs-rnd`|EvoDAG|7.1|
|`ads-rnd`|EvoDAG|7.6|
|`MLP`|scikit-learn|8.2|
|`DecisionTree`|scikit-learn|9.0|
|`LogisticRegression`|scikit-learn|10.6|
|`KNeighbors`|scikit-learn|10.6|
|`LinearSVC`|scikit-learn|10.7|
|`AdaBoost`|scikit-learn|12.4|
|`SVC`|scikit-learn|13.5|
|`GaussianNB`|scikit-learn|13.6|
|`SGD`|scikit-learn|15.8|
|`PassiveAggressive`|scikit-learn|16.6|
|`Perceptron`|scikit-learn|16.7|
|`BernoulliNB`|scikit-learn|16.9|
|`NearestCentroid`|scikit-learn|17.7|

The default EvoDAG is **fourth**, with an average rank of 6.0, behind `ExtraTrees` (4.9), `GradientBoosting` (5.5) and `RandomForest` (5.5), and ahead of every other classifier, among them the neural network (`MLP`, 8.2), a single decision tree (9.0) and the support vector machines (`LinearSVC` 10.7, `SVC` 13.5). The Friedman test says that the 21 systems are not equivalent; it does not compare pairs, so the table does not say whether the differences between neighbouring systems are significant.

EvoDAG obtains the best macro-F1 of the 21 systems on `agaricus-lepiota` and the second best on `bank`, `census-income` and `cmc`. It does poorly on the problems with many classes: on `krkopt` (18 classes) its macro-F1 is 0.25 against 0.79 of `ExtraTrees` and 0.82 of `RandomForest`, and on `letter-recognition` (26 classes) 0.65 against 0.97 of `ExtraTrees` and 0.96 of `RandomForest`. The classifiers based on decision trees do well on those problems.

## Training time

EvoDAG is slower than every classifier of scikit-learn. The table has the average rank of the time that each system takes to train, in seconds per training example (for EvoDAG, the sum over the 30 models); 1 is the fastest. Friedman test over the 30 problems: p = 2.32e-102.

|System|Family|Average rank|
|:---|:---|---:|
|`KNeighbors`|scikit-learn|2.3|
|`NearestCentroid`|scikit-learn|3.0|
|`GaussianNB`|scikit-learn|3.6|
|`BernoulliNB`|scikit-learn|4.0|
|`Perceptron`|scikit-learn|6.1|
|`DecisionTree`|scikit-learn|6.1|
|`PassiveAggressive`|scikit-learn|6.8|
|`LinearSVC`|scikit-learn|7.8|
|`SGD`|scikit-learn|8.6|
|`LogisticRegression`|scikit-learn|9.4|
|`SVC`|scikit-learn|10.5|
|`AdaBoost`|scikit-learn|11.8|
|`ExtraTrees`|scikit-learn|12.3|
|`RandomForest`|scikit-learn|13.5|
|`MLP`|scikit-learn|14.8|
|`GradientBoosting`|scikit-learn|15.3|
|`rnd-rnd`|EvoDAG|17.4|
|`fit-fit`|EvoDAG|18.3|
|`agr-rnd`|EvoDAG|18.7|
|`nvs-rnd`|EvoDAG|19.5|
|`ads-rnd`|EvoDAG|21.0|

On every problem the five EvoDAG systems are the five slowest. The times are the sum over the 30 models of the ensemble; since the models are independent they can be trained in parallel (`n_jobs`), which reduces the time you wait.

## The selection schemes

The next two tables compare EvoDAG systems that differ only in the parameters of the selection (see [Selection](selection.qmd)). Each system is named by those parameters, `<parent>-<negative>`, with two optional parts:

* **`<parent>`** is the value of `selection`: `fit` is `"fitness"`, `rnd` is `"random"`, `agr` is `"agreement"`, `sim` is `"cosine"`, `prs` is `"pearson"`, `ads` is `"angle"` and `nvs` is `"novelty"`.
* **`<negative>`** is how the individual that leaves is chosen: `fit` is `negative_selection=True` (a tournament on fitness) and `rnd` is `negative_selection=False` (random).
* **`--fit`** after the negative selection means `first_selection="fitness"`; without it the first argument is random (`first_selection="random"`; `fit-fit`, `rnd-rnd` and `nvs-rnd` do not use it).
* **`-all`** at the end means `heuristic_functions="all"`, the heuristic applied to every function with more than one argument; without it `heuristic_functions="tailored"`.

For example `agr-rnd` is `selection="agreement"`, `negative_selection=False`, `first_selection="random"`, `heuristic_functions="tailored"`: the default of classification. `fit-fit` is the classical selection, a tournament on fitness for the arguments and for the individual that leaves. All the systems use `fitness_function="macro-F1"` and `random_generations=0`.

### Combinations of parent and negative selection

Fitness, random, cosine, Pearson and agreement for the parents; fitness or random for the individual that leaves; and the three heuristics also applied to every function (`-all`). Friedman test over the 30 problems: p = 1.91e-05.

|Combination|Average rank|
|:---|---:|
|`agr-fit`|4.9|
|`agr-rnd-all`|5.1|
|`agr-fit-all`|5.1|
|`rnd-rnd`|5.1|
|`agr-rnd`|5.6|
|`sim-fit`|5.8|
|`prs-fit-all`|5.8|
|`prs-rnd-all`|6.6|
|`sim-rnd`|6.7|
|`prs-fit`|7.1|
|`fit-fit`|7.3|
|`prs-rnd`|7.4|
|`sim-fit-all`|8.6|
|`sim-rnd-all`|8.6|

The top four are variants of the agreement (`agr-fit`, `agr-rnd-all` and `agr-fit-all`) and `rnd-rnd`, the selection of every argument at random, with ranks between 4.9 and 5.1. The default configuration, `agr-rnd`, is **fifth** of the 14, with 5.6; `agr-fit`, the agreement with a tournament on fitness for the individual that leaves, is first with 4.9. The classical `fit-fit` is eleventh with 7.3. Applying the cosine to every function (`sim-rnd-all`, `sim-fit-all`) is last. Only the Friedman test was computed: the table says that the 14 combinations are not equivalent, not which pairs differ.

### Selection schemes

Fifteen systems: some of the combinations of the previous table, Angle-Driven Selection (`ads`), Novelty Search (`nvs`) and the variants that choose the first argument by fitness (`--fit`). Friedman test over the 30 problems: p = 0.000228.

|Scheme|Average rank|
|:---|---:|
|`agr-fit`|4.6|
|`rnd-rnd`|4.8|
|`agr-rnd`|5.1|
|`sim-fit`|6.3|
|`agr-fit--fit`|6.6|
|`sim-rnd`|6.6|
|`nvs-rnd`|6.8|
|`agr-rnd--fit`|7.0|
|`fit-fit`|7.0|
|`prs-fit`|7.2|
|`ads-rnd`|7.3|
|`prs-rnd`|7.6|
|`ads-fit--fit-all`|8.5|
|`ads-fit--fit`|8.7|
|`ads-rnd-all`|9.3|

In this table `agr-fit` (4.6) and `rnd-rnd` (4.8) are the best-ranked and `agr-rnd` is third with 5.1; the classical `fit-fit` is ninth with 7.0 (tied with `agr-rnd--fit`), Novelty Search (`nvs-rnd`) is seventh with 6.8 and the variants of Angle-Driven Selection are between 7.3 and 9.3. Again, only the Friedman test was computed.
